name: Coping with uncertainty in markets
purpose: How do audiences judge “what is it?” and “how good is it?”

parts.label: Complex / credence goods
points: Quality hard to assess before experience

parts.label: Market intermediaries
points: Reviews, ratings, rankings, certifications, accreditations, degrees

name: Organizational identity
purpose: Who are we as an organization?

parts.label: Centrality
points: Attributes that make the organization what it is

parts.label: Durability
points: Attributes rooted in its history, enduring over time

parts.label: Distinctiveness
points: Attributes that separate it from similar organizations

parts.label: Two positioning axes
points: Vertical: status claim (perceived quality, low/middle/high tier)

apply: List central, durable and distinctive attributes from the case
Ask whether a move reinforces or contradicts them – and how each audience reacts

name: Categorical imperative
purpose: Why can being different be penalized?

parts.label: Two-stage valuation
points: 1. Conform to a category to get attention

parts.label: Illegitimacy discount
points: Firms spanning industries get less analyst coverage → lower valuation

parts.label: Bias against creativity
points: People desire but reject novel ideas (Mueller et al. 2012)

parts.label: Generalists vs specialists
points: Softened by audience expertise/goals, actor's status, category novelty

name: Category spanning & the ambiguity paradox
purpose: Is combining several categories an asset or a liability?

parts.label: Liability
points: Confusion at the point of sale

parts.label: Asset
points: Options to pivot, valued by VCs

parts.label: Demand side
points: + resources for complex issues, diluted risk

parts.label: Supply side
points: + economies of scope, market power, risk dilution

example: Oura options: A sleep specialist · B clinical device · C luxury wearable · D create the smart-ring category · E one core, many frames.

name: Optimal distinctiveness
purpose: How different should a firm be?

parts.label: Orchestration
points: Compensatory: deviate strongly on one dimension, conform on another

parts.label: Stakeholder multiplicity
points: Customers, investors, regulators, employees judge differently

example: Askin & Mauskapf (2017): balanced songs most likely to be hits (inverted U). Berger & Packard (2018): lyrical differentiation helps, but depends on genre.

parts.label: Categories hierarchize
points: Membership signals who one is, worth and rank (Bourdieu)

parts.label: Orchestras
points: Conductors conform selectively: Katims (low) original, Ormandy (middle) conventional, Stokowski (high) deviant
